# Podcast 2 Evidence Stacking: transcript

Source: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\Old bull performance\Video_Transcripts\Podcast 2 Evidence Stacking.mp3`. Course post: https://www.oldbullperformance.com/products/running-the-room-building-a-performance-operating-system/categories/2160474409/posts/2199109505. Duration: 00:18:21. Machine-generated with faster-whisper small.en, CPU int8. This is an unverified draft; names and technical terms may be misrecognized. Timestamps refer to the downloaded media.

**00:00:00–00:00:22** Hi and welcome to this podcast. This is Podcast 2 from the Decision to Data series, How Much

**00:00:22–00:00:31** is Enough to Act. So this podcast is about practical way to avoid emotional single signal

**00:00:31–00:00:37** decisions, especially around injury by building an evidence stack and applying the statistics we've

**00:00:37–00:00:42** talked about before, baseline, small, worthwhile change, et cetera, and decide what's real versus

**00:00:42–00:00:49** what is noise. So in this episode, I want to take a bit of a different angle on the course thus far.

**00:00:49–00:00:55** Instead of asking specifically just how much is enough to act, I think a better question from a

**00:00:55–00:01:02** practical perspective is do we have sufficient information to act? So this podcast connects all

**00:01:02–00:01:09** the course labs from Module 2, but we're really having a look at some practical examples of how

**00:01:09–00:01:16** this can go. So make this explicit, this is about decision quality in high performance environments.

**00:01:16–00:01:21** So have a think about this. One ugly looking mechanism doesn't automatically mean the worst

**00:01:21–00:01:28** diagnosis. So this example I'd like to share with you was literally from only the end of 2025,

**00:01:28–00:01:33** just before Christmas. I had a player call me up that I've worked with before. I actually

**00:01:33–00:01:38** worked with him through an entire ACL reconstruction. He has actually a bistere,

**00:01:38–00:01:44** a bilateral ACL history. His most recent being in 2022, a left. And he's played since he returned

**00:01:44–00:01:50** to play. When was that issue? I'm not going to specifically discuss the rehab. However,

**00:01:50–00:01:56** most recently, he's playing as a forward, in professional soccer. He's gone forward for the

**00:01:56–00:02:02** ball, slid forward with his right leg, and his left shoulder got caught underneath him and dragged

**00:02:02–00:02:09** behind him a little bit and pulled his knee into valgus. So looking at the video, there was

**00:02:09–00:02:15** unquestionably a mechanism that didn't look great. It was a little bit ugly. However,

**00:02:15–00:02:21** the foot was being dragged and he wasn't weight bearing at the time. So my first read of it was,

**00:02:21–00:02:26** okay, looks like there's a bit of a valgus moment there. There's some medial stress. So

**00:02:26–00:02:31** you could anticipate possibly a medial ligament injury. Worst case scenario yet,

**00:02:31–00:02:37** it could be ACL. But as weird as it looked, it certainly wasn't loaded. It wasn't a classic

**00:02:37–00:02:42** ACL mechanism. Straight away, I was already starting to take that information and

**00:02:44–00:02:48** almost build a priority. So build a concept of what I thought was happening.

**00:02:49–00:02:54** Basically, what happened from there, he got up, he was a bit ginger. And I will tell you that

**00:02:54–00:02:59** listening to the commentators, it was horrific. They thought he was gone. But it was about the

**00:02:59–00:03:04** 30 minute mark in a game. He got up, he got moving, he played the 10 minutes to halftime.

**00:03:04–00:03:09** He did the whole halftime thing. So obviously you cool down a bit, you re-warm up and you

**00:03:09–00:03:14** go back out and he played the second half. So straight away, there's your second bit of evidence.

**00:03:14–00:03:20** Yes, we have a mechanism that's not great, but he was able to continue on. So what you've got

**00:03:20–00:03:26** to understand is that already we've got information. We haven't got a diagnosis, but we've got some

**00:03:26–00:03:31** pretty solid information that guy was able to play. And as a clinical sign goes, that's a

**00:03:31–00:03:37** pretty big one. So after this incident happened, he's run me up and he said, listen, our doctors

**00:03:37–00:03:41** have had a look at it straight after the game. They just said straight away, you're out. You're

**00:03:41–00:03:48** out. You've got an ACL injury. They tested him. I think they were still a relatively strong

**00:03:48–00:03:52** endpoint on the anterior draw. But the doctors were going straight to him saying you're out.

**00:03:52–00:03:56** And they went straight to the coach and said, he's out. And this is at the time,

**00:03:56–00:04:03** he was this guy's the leading goalscorer for this team. So it's a big hit for the coach to cop

**00:04:03–00:04:07** straight after the game, this guy's out. So the docs have gone straight up and out. Now,

**00:04:07–00:04:13** here's where the bias comes in. The team had had a couple of ACL injuries recently. So the doctor

**00:04:13–00:04:18** and the physio were already wound up in paranoid. And so they've gone straight with

**00:04:18–00:04:23** an emotional response. Now, I'm going to tell you for the most part, docs are pretty solid.

**00:04:23–00:04:28** They've got a good education. But I am here to tell you, if you're going to lead a department,

**00:04:28–00:04:33** if you're already leading one, or if you aspire to lead one, you have to understand

**00:04:33–00:04:39** that a doctor is human. And in sport, because we all get pressure, we all get pressure from

**00:04:39–00:04:43** the coach, and sometimes from higher ups, CEOs and the like, there's no doubt,

**00:04:43–00:04:50** they were on edge. And so they've just gone, no, he's out. But they can get biased. But as

**00:04:50–00:04:55** a leader, you've got to remain clinical. So this story progresses, the athlete went on

**00:04:55–00:05:01** and had radiological scans, we had some signal on ACL, but there was no ACL damage, nothing, no

**00:05:01–00:05:06** surrounding structures, nothing was reported, no medical damage, no middle ligament damage or

**00:05:06–00:05:13** signal. So he's just had a little bit of signal in the ACL. The response was after 12 hours,

**00:05:13–00:05:18** he's over the fully hop. Yes, he's got an ugly mechanism. Yes, he's gone on and played the

**00:05:18–00:05:24** game. The next day, he's had an MR which shows some signal, but he's able to hop. So now we're

**00:05:24–00:05:30** starting to stack information. We're not reacting to one dramatic input. Now, as far as that goes,

**00:05:30–00:05:36** the athletes run me and said, listen, what do you think, right? He said, then I can do X, Y,

**00:05:36–00:05:42** and Z. X, Y, and Z is what I'd call, in this case, athlete-led functional testing,

**00:05:42–00:05:47** which is not ideal, but it still serves a purpose. This athlete had been training,

**00:05:47–00:05:52** I finished the rehab with him in 2022. He had a few groin injuries after that. Interesting,

**00:05:52–00:06:00** there's an interesting basic side story here about how we're able to detect hip lock because

**00:06:00–00:06:05** he had a semi-memonosis graft on that side. So the hamstring injury had created some hip lock

**00:06:05–00:06:11** issues that we hadn't been able to solve, but we're able to keep them under control by constant

**00:06:11–00:06:16** training and using hip dominant stability activities like finger leg work. So more

**00:06:16–00:06:22** than squatting, he was doing Bulgarians and the like, and then dynamic variants of that and a few

**00:06:22–00:06:28** other bits and pieces that maybe we can share at some point. However, what the athlete did from

**00:06:28–00:06:35** about 2023 onwards was he just went back to those drills, to all those sessions that we'd done.

**00:06:35–00:06:40** We built those up and pretty much we came to the conclusion. We're just going to keep rotating

**00:06:40–00:06:44** through that while he's training. He's been away and played overseas. He's still leading,

**00:06:44–00:06:49** as I said, leading goal scorer, but he'd basically been tracked. So he was still doing ACL type work,

**00:06:49–00:06:54** particularly he was doing drop jumps and decelerations, drops off a box,

**00:06:54–00:07:00** I'd all start hops for distance. So he knew exactly where he was at. So he was able to

**00:07:00–00:07:05** run his own check. So he said to me, listen, I can hop and I can do this. My strength's where

**00:07:05–00:07:10** this is where it's at. And so I said to him like, what was your three hop sequence?

**00:07:10–00:07:16** Now, this is where it comes into being the practitioner you want to be. I knew straight

**00:07:16–00:07:22** away before I even asked the question, this kid doesn't answer 6.2, we've got a problem.

**00:07:22–00:07:28** So if it's 6.2, I would take as a mean, probably anything below 6, I'm going to start saying

**00:07:28–00:07:34** there's a, there might be something there. What does he say? He goes, I jump 6.2. How

**00:07:34–00:07:37** many times have you done it? He said, I've done it four times. So straight away, there's

**00:07:37–00:07:42** my next signal. From a clinical perspective, he's been able to get his strength tests,

**00:07:42–00:07:46** his strength training back up and going in a handful of days since the incident,

**00:07:46–00:07:52** and has demonstrated one of the classic ACL clearance tests, which is a three hop sequence,

**00:07:52–00:07:59** not crossover, just straight line with the controlled hops landing on the last hop.

**00:07:59–00:08:05** So what have we got? We've got known tests. We've got known baselines. We've got history,

**00:08:05–00:08:12** all useful decisions for context. Now my question is, how much data is enough to act? Do we have

**00:08:12–00:08:20** enough data to stay conclusively? We're in a position to move forward. Now, because of

**00:08:20–00:08:24** the information he'd given me, because of what I knew about him, and because of what he was able

**00:08:24–00:08:29** to relay to me, I said to him quite confidently, you need to go back because some of their medical

**00:08:29–00:08:33** staff was still saying you shouldn't play. That was ridiculous. I said, we need to push

**00:08:33–00:08:38** on and do some on field tests. He was able to report a few days later all the standard agility

**00:08:38–00:08:43** tests he passed for that issue. I said, the next challenge is just can you execute in training at

**00:08:43–00:08:48** an appropriate pace and not fatigue, which he was able to do and pressed only. So it's about

**00:08:48–00:08:54** stacking information. It's about stacking data so that you can increase the probability,

**00:08:54–00:09:01** the likelihood that this thing's okay. Looking at one data point is fraught with danger,

**00:09:01–00:09:05** fraught with danger. To that end, I think you've got to have that structure in place.

**00:09:05–00:09:12** I think when you're establishing a team, and I've heard particularly in the US football domain at

**00:09:12–00:09:18** the moment, there's whole staff changing over. So if you're walking in the door to that and

**00:09:18–00:09:24** you're in charge, I would be sitting down with the whole team saying, right, this is where we're

**00:09:24–00:09:28** at. This is what we will be doing. Yes, we'll get input from them and we'll build it and we

**00:09:28–00:09:35** can do it in a way that makes everybody comfortable. But the reality is most football teams in the US

**00:09:35–00:09:39** are starting at the time of me recording this podcast. They're starting in less than a week.

**00:09:39–00:09:44** So you've got staff who aren't even on site yet. So you need to come in and say,

**00:09:44–00:09:48** this is the way it's going to be until we can get to something else. But you need that

**00:09:48–00:09:54** simple evidence framework to be able to map the case and take it forward. If you take the

**00:09:54–00:10:00** example I used before, my CM squared thing, control movement capacity maximum, we can use that.

**00:10:00–00:10:06** Let's start with control. Has he got single joint control? Has he got control of the knee?

**00:10:06–00:10:12** Yes. We step that up. Can we do movement? Can we sequence the hip, the knee, and the ankle together

**00:10:12–00:10:19** in simple activities? Yes. Okay. Let's demonstrate capacity. Has he got the capacity to produce

**00:10:19–00:10:26** our hops when the three hops use? Yes, we do. So we're not guessing. We're checking the fundamental.

**00:10:26–00:10:34** So here's a quick checklist for you. Now, this is not brain surgery, but it feels to me like some

**00:10:34–00:10:40** groups aren't really looking at this because on my speed-sick journey, I keep getting information

**00:10:40–00:10:45** back when people haven't followed this. So let's look at these six checks. Keep it simple.

**00:10:45–00:10:51** Number one mechanism. Was there a plausible mechanism? Did we see some? Was there something

**00:10:51–00:10:56** importantly on video that we can review and say, okay, we think there's something there?

**00:10:56–00:11:01** Next one is radiological findings. No doubt. We're going to have a look at that. But no matter which

**00:11:01–00:11:07** way you look at it, radiology is still an interpretive science. You're getting a picture

**00:11:07–00:11:11** and the radiology is going to have a look and they're going to interpret it the way they see

**00:11:12–00:11:16** it, particularly when there's some gray in it. If the leg's broken, you're going to see it. It's

**00:11:16–00:11:22** broken. But when we start looking at tissue disruption and ligaments disruption, there's

**00:11:22–00:11:29** going to be the staff will grade it. And there's always some subjective elements, which is fine.

**00:11:29–00:11:33** We're going to take that information and we're going to add it to what we already know.

**00:11:33–00:11:38** So we get to three. Clinical exam. One of the most important for mine. And for

**00:11:38–00:11:43** S&P coaches who are looking to lead, you need to work with Medikos, physios in particular,

**00:11:43–00:11:50** to understand clearance tests. So when they come in clinical exam, if they come in and they've got

**00:11:50–00:11:55** no movement in the knee, they can't extend it for you. They're limping. They've got no flexion

**00:11:55–00:12:00** extension. Bad sign. If they've got joint effusion, bad sign. But in the case of the knee we just

**00:12:00–00:12:04** talked about, the athlete came in with full range of motion, full anterior draw test,

**00:12:04–00:12:10** which is main test for ACL, and no effusion. So those things are tick, tick, tick. Fundamental

**00:12:10–00:12:15** movement control checks, which we just talked through. Then we get up to capacity. Have they

**00:12:15–00:12:20** got the ability to do XYZ, the clearance tests that are appropriate for the injury we're discussing.

**00:12:20–00:12:25** Then we go to performance, relevant functional tests. Can we go on the field? Can we start

**00:12:25–00:12:29** to move? So out of the six in the example that I just gave you, he only failed one.

**00:12:29–00:12:35** He passed all the others. So by having that checklist and removing the emotion, particularly

**00:12:35–00:12:41** when emotions are high, people have been injured, and what will happen at some point in your career,

**00:12:41–00:12:46** you'll end up with a sequence of injuries that all sometimes feel like they're the same,

**00:12:46–00:12:53** what they may be. And that would take a particular analysis of your own environment.

**00:12:53–00:12:56** There's plenty of times where I've seen a run of injuries that are not related,

**00:12:56–00:13:02** but they are the same type of injury. So there's a falsehood to there being a trend. However,

**00:13:02–00:13:08** this is where we've got to make the connection. So we've got to take the test that we need,

**00:13:08–00:13:11** the test that we have, and we've got to understand their thresholds to interpret them.

**00:13:11–00:13:16** Then we've got to make sure that we can stack enough of them together to increase that

**00:13:16–00:13:22** probability that we're on the right path. So make sure you go back through all the data.

**00:13:22–00:13:27** Make sure you've got profiles from the outset. Establish the standard deviations in the smallest

**00:13:27–00:13:32** worthwhile change for the athlete. Because you've already tested the individual test

**00:13:32–00:13:37** themselves, you know what the margins of signal error are in those tests. So you need to create

**00:13:37–00:13:42** that bridge from the data to the decision. And having done that in advance, you're going

**00:13:42–00:13:49** to be in a far, far stronger place to get things moving and keep them level. We get emotion out of

**00:13:49–00:13:53** the discussions by saying, this is what we're going to do. This is how we're going to proceed.

**00:13:53–00:13:59** Now, from that perspective, I have a fantastic story from a couple of years ago. So a guy who

**00:13:59–00:14:05** worked for me for many years on my staff came up through the development level, went through rehab,

**00:14:05–00:14:10** became a senior coach. He was now a high performance manager of his own club running

**00:14:10–00:14:15** his own department. So he had a big hamstring injury in the AFL a number of years ago.

**00:14:15–00:14:19** So the athletes had this clear mechanism. Yeah, it looks like he's done something,

**00:14:19–00:14:25** but the temporal component too is he's three weeks before finals. The incident happens three

**00:14:25–00:14:32** weeks before finals. So then the doctors reacted poorly. He's gone straight up off the bat,

**00:14:32–00:14:36** told the staff, told the coach, he's out. He's out of finals. He's no chance.

**00:14:36–00:14:43** Which everybody is clearly deflated, but the difference is the HPM manager, my friend,

**00:14:43–00:14:48** went straight back in. He went into staff and he went into the coach and said, stop.

**00:14:48–00:14:53** We're going to take our time on this. We're going to have a look at it now. The punch line to this

**00:14:53–00:14:58** really is that it happens on a Saturday. It was Sunday morning. He comes in, the athlete comes in,

**00:14:58–00:15:02** and with a big hamstring, clinically, if the athlete walks in and can't walk,

**00:15:02–00:15:06** they can't straighten their leg. Yeah, you've probably got a big tendon problem.

**00:15:07–00:15:11** Now, in this case, the athlete walks in the next day, you can walk fine.

**00:15:11–00:15:18** He's got a good range of motion. So the clinical signs are there that maybe the radiology is not

**00:15:18–00:15:22** that one. And I probably skip a step down the story. They had the radiology. They're saying

**00:15:22–00:15:26** there's signal. There's some signal in the tendon, but it's not conclusive. The clinical

**00:15:26–00:15:31** sign is really good. So my man, the HPM sees the coach, sees the staff, and says, right,

**00:15:31–00:15:35** we are going to go one step at a time. We're going to be as aggressive as possible

**00:15:35–00:15:40** with treatment, and we're going to go one step at a time because we have all the data.

**00:15:40–00:15:47** We know what this guy can do. So we're going to be able to match him up step by step through

**00:15:47–00:15:52** the process with where he's at. And the one that he laid on me was, and he put to them,

**00:15:52–00:15:56** we've got his v-sig profile. So as soon as he gets back on the field, we're going to know

**00:15:57–00:16:01** exactly where he's at. And this isn't the first time I've seen this. So they got the

**00:16:01–00:16:04** athlete through, went through all the steps, grasped him as quick as possible, as quick

**00:16:04–00:16:08** as the data would suggest he was capable. But they got him to run. And from day one,

**00:16:08–00:16:14** even running at 5.5 meters per second, he was matching up with the data they had before.

**00:16:14–00:16:18** So this is about finding the gap. So they used SpeedSeek to answer a question.

**00:16:18–00:16:22** Yes, all the markers had told them they were going well. The strength markers,

**00:16:22–00:16:26** they've done isometrics, they've done eccentrics, they've done stress shortening

**00:16:26–00:16:30** cycle, hops, jumps, et cetera. But they got on the field, and this was always my argument.

**00:16:30–00:16:35** The athlete could run at BDX, let's say 5.5 meters per second. But my question is,

**00:16:35–00:16:40** how are they doing it? Have they changed? In this case, it's a big injury, and we've got no time.

**00:16:40–00:16:45** We need to know. So at 5.5 meters per second, he's running the same way that he did before

**00:16:45–00:16:50** the injury. Your confidence now is starting to climb. The probability that this athlete's

**00:16:50–00:16:55** going to be okay is increasing every day. And as he went on, he went up to step across a couple

**00:16:55–00:17:04** of weeks to full speed. His speed signal was the same the whole way. So they had

**00:17:04–00:17:08** high confidence. They sent him back in, he played. I think he missed the first final,

**00:17:08–00:17:12** then he played, and he didn't miss a game after that until the team one came out of the finals.

**00:17:14–00:17:21** That's a story where you're seeing a practical use of stacking data, getting evidence the whole

**00:17:21–00:17:27** way through. But in that sense as well, making sure you fill the gaps, not leaving a huge gap

**00:17:27–00:17:32** from the gym when you're doing all your testing in the facility too, just using GPS, which is

**00:17:32–00:17:37** the species story, of course. But it was highly effective for that group. So to close that out,

**00:17:37–00:17:44** leaders have got to protect your department from single signal reactions. You've got to use the

**00:17:44–00:17:50** evidence stack, create an evidence stack, get that information on top of one another to build

**00:17:50–00:17:54** your confidence, apply it within athlete thresholds, understand that you're not looking at noise,

**00:17:54–00:17:59** you're looking at real signal, so you can say what's real. So the real question isn't how

**00:17:59–00:18:06** much is enough. It's whether you have sufficient information to act. Focus on your evidence stack

**00:18:06–00:18:15** and good luck.

file.content:
# Podcast 2: Evidence Stacking

**Source:** Locally transcribed course audio (about 18 minutes). Timestamps are approximate. The transcript is an automated draft and has not been checked against the audio.

The central question is whether the staff have **enough independent, relevant information to act**. The speaker argues that a dramatic single result or initial impression should prompt further investigation, not settle a decision. An evidence stack combines the event or problem history, clinical findings where relevant, an athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance in the conditions the decision concerns.

- **00:00–02:20 — Resist single-signal reactions.** The speaker frames evidence stacking as a way to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence.
- **02:20–10:30 — Soccer injury anecdote.** After an awkward knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL injuries, the speaker describes comparing the initial concern with imaging, clinical examination, movement, a known individual triple-hop baseline, agility, and subsequent training exposure. The point is to update the working assessment as different kinds of evidence arrive. The anecdote does not establish that a hop distance can diagnose an injury or clear an athlete to play.
- **10:30–17:35 — Hamstring return-to-play anecdote.** The speaker describes a second case in which clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at like-for-like speeds. He emphasizes closing the gap between controlled tests and the demands of the field. The reported return to competition is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.
- **17:35–18:15 — Leadership application.** Build within-athlete reference points, identify what each new measure adds, and protect the department from changing course on one isolated signal. Ask whether the stack is sufficiently complete for the specific decision.

**Practical takeaway:** Define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that add distinct evidence. Medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions; these stories illustrate the reasoning approach rather than a clinical protocol.

# Module 2: Turning Technology Into Defensible Decisions

Module 2 argues that technology is an accelerator of good practice, not a source of it, and that a department only gets value from its tools when each one sits inside a designed workflow that ends in a decision. The five labs build a single chain: separate what a tool measures from what staff infer (2A), map every technology to the question it answers and the people who own each step (2B), decide in advance whether a metric is being monitored for short-term status or tested for long-term progress (2C), pre-agree the checkpoints where results become go, modify, or stop calls (2D), and quantify measurement noise so those checkpoints hold up under pressure (2E). Podcast 2 and its companion blog close the module with two case studies showing that no single signal, whether a scary video clip or a scan, should decide an outcome; the right question is "do we have sufficient information to act?" The module's consistent leadership message is that structure set up before pressure arrives is what protects staff, coaches, and athletes from emotional single-signal reactions.

## Lessons

### Lab 2A: Measurement vs Inference (video 6:17; PDF "What Is the Role of Technology?", 4 pp.)

- Technology became "furniture" for anyone who entered high-performance sport after about 2010; because it is normal, people stop thinking about what it actually does and start over-claiming what it can tell them (PDF p.1).
- Core principle: "Technology accelerates practice. It does not create practice." The foundation is still biology, adaptation, progressive load, recovery, and time (PDF p.1). The video attributes the accelerator idea to Jim Collins's Good to Great (transcript ~00:39).
- Measurement is what the tool directly captures: force over time (force plates), distance and speed estimates (GNSS/GPS), displacement and velocity (linear transducers), task outcomes such as jump height or sprint time. Inference is what staff think it implies: tissue stress, readiness, "neural fatigue," "healed tissue," injury risk (PDF pp.1-2).
- A force plate can say a jump changed; it cannot say the central nervous system is compromised. GPS can say external work changed; it cannot say what stress the tissue experienced (PDF p.2).
- Humans are redundant systems. The same output can hide a different strategy, so the question is never only "did they hit the number?" but "how did they hit the number, and what happens when we expose them again?" (PDF p.2).
- Matching a previous NordBord score is a valuable data point, not a clearance decision by itself (PDF p.3). The fix is triangulation plus probabilistic language.

### Lab 2B: Capability and Workflow Audit (video 4:35; PDF 3 pp.)

- Small environments align naturally because everyone talks daily. As staff, tools, and handoffs grow, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (PDF p.1).
- Capability audit is "tool truth": what it measures, what it does not measure, where its output turns into inference. Workflow audit is where most departments fail: who captures, how it is processed (vendor, in-house code, SpeedSig, dashboards), who interprets, how it is communicated, where the decision gets made (PDF p.1).
- Strategy is the highway (direction, standards, key questions). Tactics are lane changes (which tool, how to adjust tests, timing, exposure). The goal is tactical freedom inside strategic alignment; the video calls this leading by strategic intent and links it to special forces leadership (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~01:08).
- The payoff is a leadership asset: clarity and onboarding for staff, discipline for the department, a clean budget argument for what is missing, and documented procedures for performance review (PDF p.3).
- The matrix is repeatable and travels with you across clubs; technologies change over time but not overnight (PDF p.3).

### Lab 2C: Monitoring vs Testing (video 8:13; full and Free Version are byte-identical; PDF 3 pp.)

- Monitoring is short-term (days to weeks) and asks "has something changed right now?" It informs load adjustments, recovery, exposure progression or regression, and short-term risk. "Monitoring is status and trend" (PDF p.1).
- Testing is longer reach (weeks to months) and asks "have we improved capacity across a training phase?" Pre-season start vs end, block one vs block two, year one vs year five. "Testing is progress" (PDF p.1).
- Do not misuse methods. Rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are good at "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week?" but not at phase-to-phase change; because the reference moves with the data, a slow decay never falls outside the bounds of normal (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~02:13). Long-term change needs pre vs post or block vs block comparisons; the video mentions something as simple as an ANOVA (transcript ~02:56).
- The procedure rule: start with the quality you want to evaluate, decide whether you are monitoring or testing, then choose the technology, then assign it to a schedule. "We have force plates, so we should jump" is technology-led practice and creates noise (PDF p.2).
- Communicate to coaches before pressure arrives using five questions: what are we evaluating, why, how often, what output will you receive, what will we do if it changes. "For this time commitment, here's what you get back" (PDF p.2). The video adds a margin-of-error example from AFL time trials: a two-second miss inside known reliable-change error does not trigger extra training (transcript ~06:04).
- For aspiring leaders, the video says this belongs in a "first 90 plan" for a new role (transcript ~04:48). It also references the data, information, knowledge, wisdom ladder as the paradigm for what gets pushed up to coaches (transcript ~05:22).

### Lab 2D: Decision Gates (video 4:46; PDF "Designing Decision Gates", 3 pp.)

- A decision gate is a predefined checkpoint in a workflow where agreed criteria are reviewed and a clear call is made before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop. Gates stop departments from "dumping data" on coaches and senior medical staff and hoping everyone interprets it the same way (PDF p.1).
- Decision gates already exist in everything a department does; the point is to design and control them so they create clarity instead of random data followed by a random response (transcript ~00:49).
- The most common failure is vagueness. "Hamstring injury" or "hamstring capacity" is not a gate; "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance at a defined speed band and volume" is (PDF p.1).
- Rules agreed before the pressure arrives reduce debate, especially around selection, when emotion enters the room (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:04).
- Timeframes are part of the gate. Different sports have different realities: an NFL-scale organisation may get imaging straight off the field; a lower-funded program may wait days. Set expectations early so timelines are not improvised after an injury (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:29).
- The video's framing: a gate is not just a number, it is a pathway with temporal control; "discipline equals freedom" (transcript ~04:09).

### Lab 2E: The Critical Math That Cannot Be Ignored (video 5:16; PDF 3 pp.)

- Technology provides measurement; the system provides interpretation. The one question technology has to answer with confidence is "is this change real, or is it noise?" Without the math you can collect data but cannot interpret it responsibly or build gates that hold under pressure (PDF p.1).
- Two paths: system-level reliability (can we trust the test at all?) and individual-level monitoring sensitivity (can we detect meaningful change in this athlete?) (PDF p.1).
- Reliability is the whole system, not the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, and the athlete's execution (PDF p.1).
- MDC answers "is it beyond noise?" SWC answers "is it worth caring about?" Both matter and serve different purposes (PDF p.1).
- Rate of force development is the classic noisy metric because execution consistency, onset detection choices, and small timing differences all move the number. When a metric is noisy: widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates (PDF p.2). The video's anecdote is a physio arriving with "RFD is off by 12%" when 12% sits well inside the MDC (transcript ~04:13).
- Leadership angle: if staff use tests with unknown reliability, there is no foundation for trust in any number they bring you. Rigour gives credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, and gates that work (PDF p.2).

### Podcast 2: Evidence Stacking (audio 18:21; PDF "Do We Have Sufficient Information to Act?", SpeedSig/OBP companion blog, 4 pp.)

- Reframes the series question from "how much is enough to act?" to "do we have sufficient information to act?" The most dangerous decisions in high performance are the fastest ones (PDF p.1).
- A signal can be anything: a mechanism on video, a player's reaction, a clinical test, a scan, a hop distance, a single device metric, a coach's comment, or the club's own recent injury history. The mistake is treating any one of them as the verdict (PDF p.1).
- Case 1: a professional soccer forward with bilateral ACL history has an ugly valgus mechanism on video, plays the second half, gets called "out, ACL" by staff primed by recent ACL injuries at the club, then stacks MRI with no reported ACL damage, a full hop within about 12 hours, a known 6.2 m three-hop baseline repeated four times, agility passes, and training at pace. He failed one of six checks and progressed (PDF pp.1-3).
- Case 2: an AFL hamstring three weeks before finals, doctors say "no chance," the high performance manager says "stop, one step at a time," next-day walking and range of motion are good, radiology is inconclusive, and a pre-injury SpeedSig running profile lets them confirm at 5.5 m/s that he is running the same way as before injury. He missed one final and played the rest (PDF p.3).
- Lesson from case 2: the gap is often gym testing to field performance, and generic GPS alone will not answer the "how" question (PDF p.3).
- Leadership: coaches want certainty, staff feel pressure, doctors and physios are human, recent injuries distort judgement, a run of similar injuries can create a false sense of a trend. In unstable environments (new staff, preseason in a week) the leader may need to say "this is how we will proceed; we'll refine it together" (PDF p.3).

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Measurement, Inference, Probability, Next Step (Lab 2A)

What it is: a four-part communication structure that replaces absolutes ("he's ready," "this shows neural fatigue") with labelled inference.

How to run it (PDF pp.3-4):
1. What we measured (facts). Name the tests and the direction of each result.
2. What it suggests (inference). Label it as inference.
3. How confident we are (probability). Say whether probability is improving, stable, or falling.
4. What we recommend next (progression or exposure plan).

Worked example from the PDF (p.4): "We measured five markers associated with hamstring function and running exposure. All are stable pre-to-post and again at 24 hours. Probability is improving that he is ready for the next level of exposure. Next step: controlled progression toward match demands."

The video's one-line axiom (transcript ~05:50): report what you measure, state what you infer, assign a probability, then recommend the next exposure.

What it produces: a coach-facing statement that cannot be accused of over-claiming what the tool knows.

### 2. Triangulation plan (Lab 2A)

What it is: building a case for readiness from multiple angles instead of one test returning to baseline.

Hamstring return-to-play example (PDF p.3): eccentric knee flexor strength; isometric posterior-chain strength; running exposure up to meaningful speed; movement mechanics checks where available; post-exposure response immediately and at 24 hours. The video adds isometrics at inner and outer range and at the hip, jump and hop tests on a force plate for stretch-shortening cycle, and a running mechanics profile to confirm the athlete is achieving speed in an expected way (transcript ~04:13).

Rule: if all tests are positive, exposures are tolerated, and performance holds after load, then the probability improves that the athlete is ready to progress. Probability improves is not certainty (PDF p.3).

What it produces: a 4-6 data-point plan per injury type with a built-in post-exposure check.

### 3. Capability and Workflow Matrix (Lab 2B)

What it is: a one-page grid that maps every technology to the questions it answers and the workflow that carries its output to a decision.

How to build it (PDF p.2):
1. Rows = technologies. List everything: computer and software stack, GPS/IMU, force plates, load cells and force transducers, linear transducers, video tools, wellness and subjective measures.
2. Columns = applications. Option A by domain (rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring). Option B by question (hamstring injury, calf injury, adductor/groin, speed development, maximum strength, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring).
3. Fill each cell with four items: Purpose (what question it answers), Output (the metric or report delivered), Owner (who is responsible), Workflow (capture, process, interpret, communicate, decision).

The video splits Owner further: who owns the capture, who owns the understanding and determines reliability, who maintains the upkeep (transcript ~02:31).

Worked cells (PDF pp.2-3):
- Hamstring rehab (triangulation workflow): force transducer or dynamometry gives a strength capacity trend; GPS/IMU gives exposure dose (high-speed work, accelerations); mechanics check gives strategy change vs baseline; response checks give immediate and 24-hour stability. Workflow names who runs the test, where the data lives, who processes it, how it is reported, who makes the progression decision. The video's version: physio owns capture, sports science owns the reporting template (transcript ~02:59).
- Deceleration capacity (performance workflow): GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events; data may need processing in Python, R, or SpeedSig; output is a trend report plus exposure tolerance summary; decision is programming adjustment (load, density, drill selection).

What it produces: a matrix, plus a list of gaps (questions you cannot currently answer), bottlenecks (where workflow breaks), and handoff risks (where communication fails). The video's closing test, as best the transcript can be read: if it is not in the matrix it is not in the workflow, and if it is not in the workflow it does not exist (transcript ~04:12, wording garbled).

### 4. Monitoring vs Testing procedure rule (Lab 2C)

What it is: an ordering rule that prevents technology-led practice.

Steps (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:32):
1. Start with the quality you want to evaluate (what capacity matters for this sport, coach, phase, athlete).
2. Decide whether you are monitoring it (short-term status, days to weeks) or testing it (phase change, weeks to months), or both at different times.
3. Choose the technology.
4. Assign it to a schedule inside the periodised plan. Do not make it random. Injury programs should state in advance when testing happens, with flexibility for acute availability questions.
5. Match the analysis to the horizon: rolling averages and EWMA for short-term drift; pre vs post or block vs block comparisons for phase change.

What it produces: definitions of monitoring and testing, and for each key quality a stated horizon, frequency, and output.

### 5. Coach communication script (Lab 2C)

What it is: a five-question brief to run with a new coach or staff group before data collection starts (PDF p.2).

- What are we evaluating?
- Why are we evaluating it?
- How often will we do it?
- What will you receive as output?
- What will we do if it changes?

The video's script form (transcript ~05:31): "We're evaluating X because of Y. We'll do it this often. This is when the test will occur. I'll get the information to you in this period. If we get this result, this is what we're going to do." Include margin of error so a small miss is not treated as meaningful.

What it produces: coach expectations set before a surprise result creates pressure.

### 6. Decision matrix (Lab 2C)

What it is: the bridge from a result to an action. Format (PDF p.2): if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point.

Hamstring example (PDF p.2): if eccentric knee flexor force drops meaningfully, confirm test quality and re-test; physio screen plus range-of-motion checks as indicated; adjust exposure plan; reassess response immediately and at 24 hours; progress only when stable. The video's version assigns owners (S&C and sports science confirm the test; physio does clinical strain, ROM, palpation; the S&C coach adjusts the exposure plan for 48 to 72 hours; recheck within 24 hours) (transcript ~07:00). The two versions differ slightly on timing; treat them as illustrative, not as a protocol.

What it produces: for one quality, an "if improves" action, an "if declines" action, owners for each step, and a re-check time.

### 7. Five-part Decision Gate (Lab 2D)

What it is: a predefined checkpoint with agreed criteria and a forced decision (Go / Modify / Stop).

The five parts (PDF pp.1-2):
1. What is being evaluated. Name the capacity and the contraction or task precisely: eccentric knee flexor strength, isometric hip extension strength, sprint exposure tolerance (defined speed band and volume), deceleration exposure tolerance (defined intensity and count).
2. Criteria. Pass (green): proceed. Fail (red): stop or regress. Borderline (amber): confirm, repeat, or add another data point. Also define what counts as a breach so people do not argue afterwards. The video adds that criteria must be statistically grounded: different to this person, to their history, and to the population (transcript ~01:46).
3. Decision options. Progress, Hold, Regress, Refer (to medical lead), Escalate (specialist imaging or surgical opinion). Options should reflect the sport and medical setup.
4. Ownership. Who provides inputs, who interprets results, who owns the final call. Performance and medical staff often share inputs but one role owns the decision, especially in return-to-play progression.
5. Next step. Every gate triggers immediate action with a time window. PDF examples: pass, progress to next exposure stage; fail, regress and re-test in 72 hours; borderline, repeat test plus add another measure and set the review time.

Timeframes are built in (PDF p.2): "First clinical review happens within X hours. Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met. First progression gate occurs on Day Z, assuming symptoms and function allow."

What it produces: two written gates (one performance, one rehab) each with all five parts.

### 8. Reliability and threshold concepts (Lab 2E)

What it is: the minimum statistical vocabulary underneath every gate. The course teaches definitions and a decision rule; it does not present computational formulas.

Path 1, system-level reliability (PDF p.1):
- ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient): how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials. Relative reliability.
- SEM / TE (standard error of measurement / typical error): the size of the noise in the units you care about. Absolute reliability. "SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is."
- MDC95 (minimal detectable change at 95% confidence): how much change is required to be confident the shift is beyond typical measurement noise. "MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can call it real."

Path 2, individual-level monitoring sensitivity (PDF p.1):
- Typical error / within-athlete variability, often summarised as CV% for repeated measures.
- SWC (smallest worthwhile change): the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real.

Decision logic (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:34):
- Change below MDC95: likely noise.
- Change above MDC95: likely real.
- Change above SWC: likely meaningful.
- Change above both: act with confidence.
- Change real but not meaningful: note it, watch it, do not overreact.
- Neither: treat any difference as noise.

Noisy metric rule (PDF p.2): widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates. RFD is the named example.

Note for staff use: the standard computational formulas for SEM, MDC95, and SWC are not given in the course materials; the lab expects the department to already have or compute these values for its own tests.

### 9. CM² progression: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Podcast 2)

What it is: a defensible step-by-step rehab progression. Start at the base and earn the next step (PDF p.2; transcript ~09:54).

1. Control: single-joint control, range of motion, joint tolerance (effusion, pain behaviour).
2. Movement: sequencing hip, knee, and ankle together; simple patterns before complex.
3. Capacity: clearance tests appropriate to the injury; hops, deceleration, strength outputs.
4. Maximum / Performance: sport-specific exposures; fatigue-resilient execution at relevant pace.

### 10. Six-check Evidence Stack (Podcast 2)

What it is: a checklist to remove emotion and stop a department reacting to one dramatic input. Rule: no single signal decides the outcome (PDF pp.2-4; transcript ~10:45).

1. Mechanism: was there a plausible mechanism, and what does video actually show and not show (load, weight-bearing)?
2. Radiology: use it but it is interpretive; clear structural disruption is clear, tissue "signal" needs context.
3. Clinical exam: range of motion, effusion, functional limp, key ligament tests (anterior drawer endpoint), gait.
4. Fundamental control and movement checks: can they control the joint, can they sequence cleanly?
5. Capacity tests (clearance tests): hops, deceleration, strength and SSC outputs relevant to the tissue and sport.
6. Performance-relevant functional tests: on-field movement, agility and exposure at pace, execution without breakdown under fatigue.

Count passes against fails. In the soccer case the athlete failed one of six and passed the rest, which shifted the decision from fear to probability.

### 11. Statistics-to-decision sequence (Podcast 2 blog)

Five steps (PDF p.3): test your tests (system reliability); build athlete baselines early; define thresholds (normal variation, SWC, what counts as meaningful in your world); use multiple signals; bridge data to decisions so you can say "this is what we saw, this is what it means, this is what we do next." The goal is not perfect certainty but reducing avoidable error.

## Deliverables / exercises

All deliverables are stated in the "Lab task" section of each PDF.

Lab 2A (PDF p.4):
1. A one-paragraph definition: "Technology is an accelerator because..."
2. Three measurements collected weekly, each with what is measured and what is typically inferred.
3. One example where the environment overstates certainty (CMJ fatigue, GPS load, isometrics), rewritten as measurement, inference, probability, next step.
4. A triangulation plan for one injury type (hamstring, groin, calf, knee) using 4-6 data points and a post-exposure check.

Lab 2B (PDF p.3):
1. A one-page Capability and Workflow Matrix (rows = tech, columns = applications).
2. At least 10 cells completed with purpose, output, owner, workflow steps.
3. A list of gaps, bottlenecks, and handoff risks.

Lab 2C (PDF p.3):
1. Written definitions of monitoring and testing.
2. One quality (deceleration capacity, jump performance, hamstring capacity) specified as monitored, tested, or both, with frequency and output.
3. A decision matrix: if result improves, action; if result declines, action; who owns each step; when to re-check.

Lab 2D (PDF p.3):
Two decision gates, one performance (speed exposure progression or deceleration capacity) and one rehab (hamstring return-to-run), each with key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe.

Lab 2E (PDF p.3):
1. Top 5 tests or metrics, each with ICC (if available), SEM/TE, and MDC95 or chosen decision threshold.
2. For one key monitoring metric: within-athlete variability (TE or CV%) and SWC.
3. One decision gate statement: "If change is > ___, we do ___; if not, we ___."

Podcast 2 blog (PDF pp.3-4):
- The Evidence Stack Card (copy/paste): decision question plus the six checks in order.
- Five reflection prompts: where single-signal decisions happen most in your environment; which of the six checks you skip under pressure; whether you have baseline profiles for key tests; what "one step at a time" looks like for a knee ligament incident, hamstring injury, and groin pain episode; how your evidence stack sounds when explained to a coach in 30 seconds.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology accelerates practice. It does not create practice." (Lab 2a PDF p.1)
2. "We often infer responsibly. That's part of the job. But we must label inference as inference, because overstating certainty is what drives coaches crazy." (Lab 2a PDF p.2)
3. "A device doesn't create impact. A workflow does." (Lab 2b PDF p.1)
4. "Monitoring is status and trend. Testing is progress." (Lab 2c PDF p.1)
5. "Coaches don't need more numbers. They need clarity." (Lab 2c PDF p.2)
6. "Random monitoring and testing creates random data." (Lab 2C video ~07:47)
7. "If ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions." (Lab 2D PDF p.2)
8. "A gate without a next step is just conversation." (Lab 2D PDF p.2)
9. "SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is. MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can call it real." (Lab 2E PDF p.1)
10. "If you can't quantify noise, you can't defend your decisions." (Lab 2E video ~04:57)
11. "Leadership is staying clinical when others can't." (Stacking Evidence blog p.1)
12. "No single signal decides the outcome." (Stacking Evidence blog p.4)

- Two reliability paths, ICC/SEM/TE/MDC95/CV%/SWC definitions: PDF-confirmed (2E p.1).
- MDC/SWC decision logic: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2).
- RFD as noisy metric and three responses: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2). 12% RFD anecdote: transcript-only (2E ~04:13).
- Rigour creates trust: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2).
- Evidence stack framing and signal list: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.1).
- Soccer case including 6.2 m three-hop repeated four times, MRI signal without damage, hop at ~12 hours: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.1-2). Bilateral ACL history with 2022 left: PDF-confirmed (p.1). Semimembranosus graft and hip-lock side story: transcript-only (Podcast ~05:52).
- CM² progression: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.2).
- Six checks: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.2-4).
- AFL hamstring case, 5.5 m/s SpeedSig comparison, returned after missing one final: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3).
- Five-step statistics-to-decision sequence: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3).
- Leadership in unstable environments ("this is how we will proceed"): PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3). US college football staff turnover context: transcript-only (Podcast ~09:05).
- Evidence Stack Card and reflection prompts: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.3-4).

## Applicability notes

- The Capability and Workflow Matrix maps directly onto the Applied Performance stack. Rows: Catapult GPS, VALD force plates, VALD dynamometry (NordBord, ForceFrame, DynaMo), the AMS, video, wellness. Columns by question the football and Olympic sport coaches actually ask. The matrix exposes the cells where the AMS holds data nobody acts on, and the cells where Athletic Performance captures a metric but Athletic Medicine never sees it. It also doubles as the onboarding document for new Athletic Performance staff and the budget justification for the next VALD or Catapult renewal.
- Lab 2A's NordBord example is a direct warning for VALD reporting: a returning athlete matching their pre-injury eccentric knee flexor score is one data point in a triangulation, not a return-to-play clearance. Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine should agree that the AMS return-to-play summary reports the measured markers, the inference, the confidence, and the next exposure step rather than a "cleared / not cleared" flag.
- Lab 2C forces a decision about which Catapult and VALD outputs are monitoring and which are testing. Daily CMJ on force plates and session high-speed running from Catapult are monitoring (EWMA and rolling baselines in the AMS are appropriate). Pre-camp vs post-camp or block-to-block strength and jump batteries are testing and need pre vs post comparison, not the AMS's continuous smoothing. Coaches should be told which is which before the season starts, using the five-question script.
- Lab 2E is the technical work the department owes itself. Every VALD and Catapult metric used in a decision gate needs its own ICC, SEM/TE, and MDC95 from Baylor's own equipment, protocol, testers, and environment, plus a within-athlete CV% and SWC for the monitored metrics. Vendor-published reliability is a starting point, not a substitute. Force plate RFD and other early-phase force-time metrics should be treated as noisy until proven otherwise; use wider bands or a more stable metric for gates.
- Decision gates and the decision matrix belong in the AMS as written rules with owners: what quality, what threshold in local MDC and SWC units, what options, who in Athletic Medicine owns the return-to-play call and who in Athletic Performance owns the exposure adjustment, and the re-check window. Writing timeframes into the gate (first clinical review within X hours, imaging within Y days, first progression gate on Day Z) is what stops a head coach's Sunday phone call from setting the timeline.
- The six-check evidence stack is a shared language for Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine case reviews after an in-game incident. Mechanism from film, radiology, clinical exam, control and movement, capacity tests on VALD, and performance-relevant field exposure on Catapult give both groups a structured way to say "we have five of six" instead of reacting to the clip. The AFL case shows why a pre-injury running profile from GPS matters: the return-to-run question is not only "can he hit 5.5 m/s" but "is he running the same way he did before."
